title: Logical Consistency
body:
A set of formulas is **consistent** when at least one assignment of truth values makes all of
them true at once. It is inconsistent when no assignment does.

```
{ P → Q,  P,  ¬Q }

 P  Q | P→Q |  P  | ¬Q  | all three
 T  T |  T  |  T  |  F  |    no
 T  F |  F  |  T  |  T  |    no
 F  T |  T  |  F  |  F  |    no
 F  F |  T  |  F  |  T  |    no       inconsistent
```

Consistency is a property of a set, so each member can be perfectly reasonable on its own while
the group is unsatisfiable, which is what the example shows. Finding the row that satisfies
everything is the same problem SAT solvers attack, and [[NP-Complete]] in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] is where its difficulty is classified.

An inconsistent set of premises makes an argument valid trivially, since no row makes the
premises true, so no row makes them true with a false conclusion. That is a useless kind of
validity and is why [[Soundness]] is the property worth having.
